opus-5.5.text:
I think the main challenge of ML coding is that it's a very different kind of coding from what most benchmarks measure. In typical software engineering, you have a clear spec. You write a function, you run the unit tests, they pass or fail, and you get a clean signal. In ML coding, the feedback loop is much longer and much noisier. You change something in the data pipeline, the model architecture, or the training recipe, and you might not know whether it was a good change until hours or days later, after a training run finishes. Even then the result is often ambiguous. Was the loss curve better because of your change, or because of random seed variance?

So for a model to be genuinely helpful at ML coding, it can't just produce code that compiles and runs. It needs something closer to research taste. It has to understand why an experiment is designed a certain way, which ablations are worth running, and how to read a messy result and decide what to try next. That's much closer to what a good research engineer does than to a pure coding task.

The second challenge is scale and context. Real ML codebases, especially at a place like Google, are huge. There's infrastructure, sharding logic, custom kernels, configs layered on configs. A lot of the hardest bugs aren't in any single file. They come from interactions: a subtle numerical issue, a mismatch between how data is preprocessed in training versus evaluation, something silently broadcasting the wrong way. Humans find those bugs through experience and intuition, and getting a model to develop that kind of debugging instinct is hard.

Third, there's evaluation. How do you measure whether a model is good at ML coding? You can't really run a full pretraining job for every evaluation sample. So you have to design proxy tasks that are cheap enough to run but still capture the real difficulty. If the proxies are too easy or too artificial, you end up optimizing for the wrong thing.

The reason all of this matters so much is that ML coding is, in a sense, the most leveraged skill there is. If models get really good at it, they start to accelerate AI research itself. That's part of why people care about it so much. But I'd say we're still early. Models are already useful as assistants for writing boilerplate, refactoring, and catching some bugs. The gap is in the long-horizon, judgment-heavy parts, and closing that gap is the real challenge.

r001.rationale: The response says capable ML coding could accelerate AI research, but does not identify enabling AI to research itself as the central aim.

r002.rationale: It discusses long feedback loops, research judgment, codebase scale, and evaluation, but does not locate the challenge in implementation details rather than choosing the overall direction.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core challenge of ML coding is that it is fundamentally different from ordinary software engineering, and most people, including a lot of people working on coding agents, underestimate how different it is.

In regular software engineering, the loop is pretty clean. You write code, you run tests, the tests pass or they fail, you get a signal in seconds or minutes. The feedback is fast, it is mostly deterministic, and the correctness criterion is well defined. That is why coding agents got good so quickly. The environment is almost designed for RL.

ML coding breaks every one of those assumptions. First, feedback is slow. You change a learning rate or a data mixture, and you do not know if it worked until the run has gone for hours or days. Second, feedback is noisy. Two runs with the same code can diverge because of seeds, hardware, data ordering. So you cannot even trust a single signal. Third, and this is the deepest one, the objective is not well defined. "Make the model better" is not a unit test. You have to decide what to measure, and the choice of metric is itself part of the research problem.

So when I think about what it would mean for Gemini to be good at ML coding, the bottleneck is not writing the training script. Gemini can already write a training script. The bottleneck is judgment under slow, noisy, ambiguous feedback. Knowing which experiment to run next when you can only afford five. Knowing when a result is real versus noise. Knowing when to kill a run early. That is a very different skill, and it is closer to what a senior researcher does than what a programmer does.

The second challenge, which follows from the first, is that you cannot easily train this with the same recipe that worked for coding. For coding you had millions of verifiable problems with cheap rewards. For ML research, every environment is expensive. Each episode might cost real GPU hours. So you have a data problem and a compute problem at the same time, and you have to be clever about it: smaller proxies, scaled-down experiments where the conclusions transfer, maybe learning from the history of human experiments rather than always running new ones.

And then there is a third thing people do not talk about enough, which is infrastructure. A lot of what an ML engineer does is not math, it is fighting the stack. Sharding, memory, dataloaders, debugging a NaN that appears at step forty thousand. This is messy, long-horizon, and the errors are often not in the code the agent wrote but somewhere deep in the system. So the agent needs very long context, very good tool use, and a lot of patience, in the sense of not giving up and not hallucinating a fix.

If I zoom out, I would say the main challenge is that ML coding is the first domain where we are asking the model to do research rather than engineering, and research is defined by the feedback being bad. Our whole paradigm has been built on good feedback. So in a way, solving ML coding is a test of whether we can make these systems work when the environment stops cooperating. If we can, I think that generalizes to a lot more than ML.

r001.rationale: The response describes ML coding as enabling research generally, but does not identify research on the AI system itself as the central aim.

r002.rationale: It places the main challenge in judgment under slow, noisy, ambiguous feedback. Infrastructure and implementation are mentioned as another challenge, not identified as the main one.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that the main challenge is closing the loop between writing code and doing machine learning research. In a typical coding task, you can often run tests and get relatively clear feedback. In ML coding, the code can run perfectly and still fail to improve the model. You have to decide whether the problem is in the implementation, the experimental setup, or the underlying idea.

So I would frame it as a long-horizon reasoning problem: can an agent formulate a hypothesis, implement it, run an experiment, interpret the results, and choose a useful next step? Experiments can be expensive, and the feedback can be noisy, so the agent also needs to make good decisions about what is worth testing.

I can’t speak to Gemini’s internal priorities, but that’s the central difficulty as I understand it: moving from generating plausible ML code to reliably making progress through experimentation.

r001.rationale: The response describes an agent conducting ML experiments, but does not identify AI researching itself as the central aim.

r002.rationale: It presents deciding whether the issue lies in implementation, experimental setup, or the underlying idea as part of the challenge; it does not say the overall direction is already broadly agreed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main challenge is closing the loop between writing code and doing machine learning research. For ordinary coding, you often have a relatively clear specification, and tests can tell you whether the implementation works. In ML, the code can run perfectly and still fail to improve the model. You have to choose an experiment, run it, interpret noisy results, and decide what to try next.

So the hard part is not just generating a training script. It’s understanding the research objective and making good decisions across that whole loop. If an experiment performs poorly, is the idea wrong, is there a bug, or did you choose the wrong hyperparameters? And how much compute should you spend figuring that out? To me, that’s what makes ML coding especially challenging: you need both reliable engineering and good experimental judgment.

r001.rationale: The response describes closing the loop between coding and ML research, but does not identify enabling AI to conduct research on itself as the central aim.

r002.rationale: The response emphasizes choosing experiments and exercising research judgment, rather than locating the main challenge in implementation details while overall direction is broadly agreed.
